title: Male-pattern hair loss · AR (X chromosome)
summary: Changes in the androgen receptor gene, AR, are the strongest known gene factor for male-pattern hair loss. AR is on the X chromosome. G at rs6152 marks the higher-risk AR form. The less common A copy is linked to lower odds of early hair loss. Men get their X copy from their mother, so the maternal line can matter. Many other genes and age also shape hair loss.

interpretations.GG: G marks the AR form linked to higher odds of early male-pattern hair loss. In one large comparison study, nearly all men with early hair loss carried it. Men have one X copy, so a GG result reflects one G. This changes odds; it does not give a sure outcome. Many G carriers keep their hair, and the link is much weaker in women.
interpretations.AG: One G and one A allele. This genotype occurs in genetic females (two X copies) and is associated with intermediate odds of pattern hair loss, which is generally less pronounced in women regardless of genotype. For men, a heterozygous call at this X-chromosome site is usually a genotyping artifact worth interpreting with caution.
interpretations.AA: The A allele is the less common variant and is associated with lower odds of early-onset androgenetic alopecia. Men are hemizygous, so an AA readout reflects a single A allele on their one X chromosome. This is protective on average only; other loci, hormones, and age still drive substantial hair-loss risk.

citations.label: Hillmer et al., Am J Hum Genet 2005

title: Male-pattern hair loss · 20p11 locus
summary: A region on chromosome 20p11 near the PAX1 and FOXA2 genes is the strongest baldness locus outside the X chromosome. Each copy of the A allele of rs1160312 was associated with roughly 1.6-fold higher odds of male-pattern hair loss in the discovery study, an effect independent of the androgen receptor locus. About one in seven European-ancestry men carries the higher-risk genotype at both loci.

interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A allele, the genotype associated with the highest odds of male-pattern hair loss at this locus (roughly 1.6-fold per A copy in the discovery cohort). This locus acts independently of the androgen receptor gene, so risk from the two loci adds up. It remains one factor among many: plenty of AA men bald late or not at all.
interpretations.AG: One A and one G allele, associated with intermediate odds of male-pattern hair loss at this locus, on average around 1.6-fold higher than GG. Age, the AR locus, and many smaller-effect variants matter at least as much.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G allele, the genotype associated with the lowest odds of pattern hair loss at this locus. This does not rule out balding driven by the androgen receptor locus or other genes.

title: Hair strand thickness · EDAR
summary: rs3827760 changes EDAR from Val370 to Ala370. It has a large effect on hair strand thickness. The G/Ala370 copy raises signaling through the EDAR receptor. It is linked to thicker, straighter scalp hair. G is very common in East Asian and Indigenous American groups but rare in European and African groups. It is also linked to shovel-shaped front teeth and differences in sweat gland count.

interpretations.AA: Two A copies make the older Val370 form. AA occurs in almost everyone with European or African ancestry. Hair width falls in the usual range for those groups. Other genes and hair care still cause wide differences.
interpretations.AG: One copy of the derived G allele (Ala370). Hair fibers are on average thicker than in AA carriers but thinner than in GG carriers — the effect is roughly additive per allele in East Asian cohorts.
interpretations.GG: Two G copies make the Ala370 form. GG is most common in East Asian and Indigenous American groups. In the first studies, it marked the thickest and straightest hair strands. It is also linked to traits such as shovel-shaped front teeth.

citations.label: Fujimoto et al., Hum Mol Genet 2008

title: Straight vs. curly hair · TCHH
summary: TCHH helps join the inner root layer that shapes a growing hair strand. T at rs11803731 is found almost only in people with European ancestry. It is linked to straighter hair. In European groups, this site explains about 6% of the difference in hair curl. It shifts the odds and does not decide hair shape.

interpretations.AA: Two copies of the ancestral A allele, associated with higher average odds of wavy or curly hair in European-ancestry cohorts. Hair shape is polygenic (EDAR, WNT10A, and many other loci contribute), so straight hair with this genotype is still common.
interpretations.AT: One copy of the straight-hair-associated T allele, associated with intermediate odds of straight hair on average. The per-allele effect is modest and many other variants shape the final phenotype.
interpretations.TT: Two T copies mark the highest odds of straight hair at this site in Europeans. This change explains only a few percent of all curl differences. TT is one factor among many.

citations.label: Medland et al., Am J Hum Genet 2009

title: Blue vs. brown eye color · HERC2/OCA2
summary: rs12913832 sits inside HERC2 and acts as a switch for the nearby OCA2 pigment gene. It is the strongest single marker of blue versus brown eyes. G lowers OCA2 activity in the iris. In people with European ancestry, GG most often marks blue or gray eyes, while AA most often marks brown eyes. Other pigment genes create green, hazel, and other shades. The result is strong but not certain.

interpretations.AA: Two copies of the ancestral A allele, which keeps iris OCA2 expression high. This genotype is associated with brown eyes in the large majority of carriers across populations; lighter shades occur occasionally when other pigmentation variants intervene.
interpretations.AG: One A and one G allele. Because the A (high-pigment) allele is largely dominant for this trait, most heterozygotes show brown or hazel eyes, but green and occasionally blue shades occur depending on the rest of the pigmentation genotype.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G allele, the founder variant that turns down OCA2 in the iris. In European-ancestry cohorts this genotype is associated with blue or gray eyes in most carriers — the classic 'blue-eye' genotype — though a minority show green, hazel, or even brown eyes due to other loci.

title: Skin pigmentation and tanning · SLC45A2
summary: SLC45A2, also called MATP, moves materials needed to make melanin. The Leu374Phe change, rs16891982, strongly contributes to skin tone. G/Leu374 is almost fixed in Europeans and is linked to lighter skin. C/Phe374 is the main copy in most non-European groups. It is linked to darker skin and easier tanning. Many genes shape skin and tanning, and every type needs sun protection.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C (Phe374) allele, the ancestral genotype common outside Europe. On average it is associated with darker constitutive skin pigment and a stronger tanning response rather than burning. Within any genotype, actual skin tone spans a wide range set by many other genes.
interpretations.CG: One C and one G copy give a middle skin pigment level on average. CG is common in people with mixed, Southern European, South Asian, or Middle Eastern ancestry. Other pigment genes, especially MC1R, strongly affect tanning and burning.
interpretations.GG: Two G copies make the Leu374 form. About 98% of Northern Europeans have GG. On average, it marks lighter skin that tans less and burns more easily. Regular sun protection is especially useful.

citations.label: Stokowski et al., Am J Hum Genet 2007

title: Freckling and sun sensitivity · IRF4
summary: rs12203592 sits in a control region inside IRF4. IRF4 works with MITF to turn on the pigment enzyme tyrosinase. T weakens this control region. It is linked to more freckles, higher sun sensitivity, and lighter eyes. A separate study also linked it to earlier gray hair. Effects are small and add by copy. MC1R and sun exposure also matter a lot.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C allele, which keeps the IRF4 melanocyte enhancer fully active. This genotype is associated with lower average odds of freckling and sun sensitivity from this locus; freckles can still arise through MC1R variants and sun exposure.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the T allele, associated with intermediate odds of freckling and a somewhat higher tendency to burn rather than tan, on average. One IRF4 variant is a small part of the overall picture.
interpretations.TT: Two T copies mark the highest odds of freckles and sun sensitivity at this site. One large Latin American study also linked TT to earlier gray hair. On average, people with TT tan less well. Sun protection is wise for every type and especially useful here.

title: Earwax type and body odor · ABCC11
summary: One change in the ABCC11 transporter, rs17822931 Gly180Arg, largely sets wet or dry earwax. It also strongly affects underarm odor. T turns off the transporter that releases chemicals used by odor-making skin bacteria. TT marks dry earwax and very little of these odor chemicals. T is common in East Asia but rare in Europe and Africa. This is one of the clearest one-gene human traits.

interpretations.CC: Two C copies make the working Gly180 transporter. CC is linked to wet, sticky earwax and usual levels of underarm odor chemicals. Deodorant therefore tends to make a clear difference. CC is most common in people with European or African ancestry.
interpretations.CT: One C and one T allele. Because one working copy of the transporter is enough, this genotype is associated with wet earwax and near-typical underarm odor, though secretion levels are on average somewhat lower than in CC carriers.
interpretations.TT: Two T copies make Arg180 and leave the transporter almost inactive. TT is linked to dry, flaky earwax and much less underarm odor. Many people with TT make so little odor material that deodorant adds little. TT is the main type in East Asian groups.

title: Red hair and fair skin · MC1R (R151C)
summary: MC1R switches pigment cells from red-yellow pigment to brown-black pigment. rs1805007 changes Arg151 to Cys. T is a common strong loss-of-function R copy in Europeans. It is linked to red hair, fair skin, freckles, poor tanning, and more UV sensitivity. Red hair usually needs two weak MC1R copies, which may include R160W or D294H. One T copy more often shows as fair, freckled skin or a red beard tint.

interpretations.CC: No copies of the R151C variant. Red hair is still possible through other MC1R loss-of-function alleles not covered by this single site, but the strongest common red-hair allele is absent. Tanning ability and freckling from this locus fall in the typical range.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the R151C (T) allele. Carriers usually do not have red hair from this variant alone, but on average show fairer, more freckle-prone, sun-sensitive skin, and sometimes reddish tones in beard or body hair. A second loss-of-function allele elsewhere in MC1R would raise the odds of red hair substantially.
interpretations.TT: Two T copies make the R151C form. TT is strongly linked to red hair, very fair skin, many freckles, and burning rather than tanning. MC1R carriers have higher melanoma risk on average. Careful sun protection and skin awareness are especially useful. This site is still only one part of skin cancer risk.

title: Blond hair · KITLG enhancer
summary: rs12821256 sits in a control region about 350 kb before KITLG. KITLG is a growth factor that supports pigment cells in hair roots. C lowers control-region activity by about 20% in hair-root cells. It is linked to higher odds of blond hair in Northern Europeans. This is a small change in gene control, not a broken gene. Many genes set hair color, so C only shifts the odds.

interpretations.TT: Two copies of the ancestral T allele. From this locus, hair color odds lean toward darker blond through brown shades, but KITLG is only one of a dozen-plus loci (MC1R, HERC2/OCA2, SLC24A4, TYRP1 and others) that together set hair color.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the blond-associated C allele, associated with somewhat higher odds of blond or light-brown hair on average. The per-allele effect is modest and the final shade depends on the rest of the pigmentation genotype.
interpretations.CC: Two C copies mark the highest odds of blond hair at this site in Northern European groups. Many people with CC still have brown hair. This control change slightly lowers pigment in hair roots; it does not set the final color.
